umbrellas.title: THE SIX UMBRELLAS
umbrellas.intro: Every enduring issue fits under one of these six. Spot the umbrella fast. Then name the exact issue underneath it, and explain it.

items.name: POWER & ITS ABUSE
items.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.
items.issues: Abuse of Power · Imperialism · Human Rights Violations · Inequality

issue_defs.name: Abuse of Power
issue_defs.definition: when someone with authority uses it to harm people or to serve themselves.

issue_defs.name: Imperialism
issue_defs.definition: when a stronger country takes control of another land and its people.

issue_defs.name: Human Rights Violations
issue_defs.definition: when people are denied the basic rights every person should have, like life, freedom and safety.

issue_defs.name: Inequality
issue_defs.definition: when some groups get fewer rights, chances or resources than others.

items.name: CONFLICT
items.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

issue_defs.name: Conflict
issue_defs.definition: a struggle between groups, nations or ideas, from argument to war.

items.name: IDENTITY & NATIONALISM
items.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

issue_defs.name: Nationalism
issue_defs.definition: a people's loyalty to their own nation, and the push for that nation to rule itself.

issue_defs.name: Cultural Exchange and Diffusion
issue_defs.definition: when ideas, beliefs, goods and ways of life spread from one people to another.

items.name: WEALTH & RESOURCES
items.question: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

issue_defs.name: Economic Development
issue_defs.definition: how a place grows its wealth, and who that growth helps or leaves behind.

issue_defs.name: Scarcity
issue_defs.definition: not having enough of something people need, like food, water or land.

items.name: TECHNOLOGY & ENVIRONMENT
items.question: What new tools let people do, and what they cost the world around them.
items.issues: Scientific and Technological Change · Environmental Crisis

issue_defs.name: Scientific and Technological Change
issue_defs.definition: new knowledge and tools that change how people live and work.

issue_defs.name: Environmental Crisis
issue_defs.definition: serious harm to land, air, water or climate, often caused by people.

items.name: A CONNECTED WORLD
items.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

issue_defs.name: Cooperation
issue_defs.definition: when groups or countries work together toward a shared goal.

issue_defs.name: Population and Migration
issue_defs.definition: how the number of people in a place changes, and why people move.

close: On the essay, write the exact issue, not the umbrella: “Human Rights Violations,” not “Power & Its Abuse.”
Then EXPLAIN IT: define the problem in one sentence, and show where a document shows it.

casefiles.title: 10.2 Casefile A · The Enlightenment and its reformers

docs.title: Locke on why people leave the state of nature
docs.src: Source: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government, 1690

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and what had just happened in England?
steps.line: The source line has the name and the year. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 2 says what England did the year before, and what Locke was writing to justify.
Five sentences. The first two are questions Locke asks himself, and the last three answer them. Hard words: equity means fairness, and hence means for this reason.

steps.question: Why does Locke say people leave the state of nature, and what do they get?
steps.line: Why is in his middle sentences. What they get is in his last sentence. Use Locke's words.

steps.question: How would Hobbes, in the box above Document 1, see Locke's deal?
steps.line: Reread the Hobbes box. Then ask who holds the power when each deal is done, and whether the people can ever take it back.

steps.question: What lasting problem is Locke trying to solve?
steps.line: Find the two words he uses for rights in the state of nature, near the end of his fourth sentence. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question those words fit.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 1's questions in your casefile, starting on page 4. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “If man in the state of nature is free, if he is absolute lord of his own person and possessions, why will he give up his freedom? Why will he put himself under the control of any person or institution? The obvious answer is that rights in the state of nature are constantly exposed to the attack of others. Since every man is equal and since most men do not concern themselves with equity and justice, the enjoyment of rights in the state of nature is unsafe and insecure. Hence each man joins in society with others to preserve his life, liberty, and property.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Suppose man in the state of nature (life before any government) is free. Suppose he is absolute lord (complete master) of his own person and possessions (the things he owns). Then why will he give up his freedom? Why will he put himself under the control of any person or institution (an organized group, like a government)? The obvious answer is this. In the state of nature, rights are always open to attack from others. Every man is equal. But most men do not care about equity (fairness) and justice. So in the state of nature, the enjoyment of rights is unsafe and insecure. Hence (for this reason) each man joins in society with others to preserve his life, liberty, and property.”

docs.title: Locke on a government that breaks the deal
docs.src: Source: John Locke, Two Treatises on Civil Government

steps.question: Who wrote this, and what deal from Document 1 is he talking about?
steps.line: Same writer as Document 1. The heading says this one is about a government that breaks the deal. Document 1's last sentence tells you what deal.

One long sentence, with pieces cut out where you see dots. Hard words: the legislature is the lawmakers, and forfeit is in your KEY VOCABULARY for Day 2. Watch who holds the power at the start of the sentence.

steps.question: What does Locke say happens when lawmakers grab absolute power?
steps.line: Find the word forfeit, then keep reading to the end. Find the words that say where the power goes.

steps.question: How would the lawmakers in this sentence explain what they did?
steps.line: Picture a member of that legislature reading this. Would they ever describe it the way Locke does?

steps.question: What lasting problem does this sentence warn about?
steps.line: Your clue words are in the first half of the sentence: what the legislature grabs, and how much of it. Open the Six Umbrellas and check those words against each question.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 2's questions in your casefile, starting on page 5. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “[When] the legislature shall . . . grasp [for] themselves, or put into the hands of any other, an absolute power over their lives, liberties, and estates of the people, . . . they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands for quite contrary ends, and it [passes] to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty. . . .”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Sometimes the legislature (the lawmakers) will . . . grab for themselves an absolute power (power with no limits) over the lives, liberties, and estates (property) of the people. Or they will put that power into the hands of someone else. When that happens, . . . they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands. The people gave them that power for quite contrary (opposite) ends (purposes). And it [passes] to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty. . . .” (To resume means to take back up.)

docs.title: Montesquieu on the power of judging
docs.src: Source: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

steps.question: Who was Montesquieu, and when did he write this?
steps.line: The source line gives you only a name and a book. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 3 tells you who he was and when the book came out.
Three sentences. The first sets the rule, and the next two each start with If. Hard words: arbitrary is in your KEY VOCABULARY for Day 3, and an oppressor is someone who uses power to crush people.

steps.question: What does Montesquieu say happens when judging is joined to another power?
steps.line: Look at the two sentences that start with If. Each one ends with something going wrong. Put each one in your own words.

steps.question: How would a king who makes the laws and judges the cases answer this?
steps.line: Picture that king reading the first sentence. What would he say he needs all that power for?

steps.question: What lasting problem is Montesquieu trying to prevent?
steps.line: Find the word liberty in the first sentence and the word oppressor in the last. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question they fit.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 3's questions in your casefile, starting on page 7. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “. . . Nor is there liberty if the power of judging is not separate from legislative power and from executive power. If it were joined to legislative power, the power over the life and liberty of the citizens would be arbitrary, for the judge would be the legislator. If it were joined to executive power, the judge could have the force of an oppressor. . . .”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “. . . There is no liberty if the power of judging is not separate from legislative power (the power to make laws) and from executive power (the power to carry out laws). If it were joined to legislative power, the power over the life and liberty of the citizens would be arbitrary (decided by one person's will, not by law). That is because the judge would be the legislator (the lawmaker). If it were joined to executive power, the judge could have the force of an oppressor (someone who uses power to crush people). . . .”

docs.title: Montesquieu on powers united in one person
docs.src: Source: Baron de Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws

steps.question: Who wrote this, and what did he do for a living?
steps.line: Same writer as Document 3. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 3 says who he was, and the source line names his book.
One sentence, with two hard words explained in the brackets. Read it in two halves: up to the word liberty, then the reason after because. Here, execute means carry out.

steps.question: What does Montesquieu say is lost when two powers sit in the same hands, and why?
steps.line: Find the word united. Then read past the word because to find his reason.

steps.question: Montesquieu was a noble. Whose view of power might be different from his?
steps.line: He names a monarch or senate. Picture someone with no power at all reading this, a peasant in France. What would worry them most?

steps.question: What lasting danger is he pointing at?
steps.line: One clue word shows up twice in the second half of the sentence. Open the Six Umbrellas and check it against each question.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 4's questions in your casefile, starting on page 8. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates [government officials], there can be no liberty; because apprehensions [fears] may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws to execute them in a tyrannical manner. . . .”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Sometimes the legislative and executive powers (the power to make laws and the power to carry them out) are united in the same person. Or they are united in the same body of magistrates [government officials]. When that happens, there can be no liberty. Why? Because apprehensions [fears] may arise. People may fear that the same monarch or senate will enact (pass) tyrannical laws (cruel, unfair laws). Then they will execute (carry out) them in a tyrannical manner. . . .”

docs.title: Rousseau states the problem the social contract solves
docs.src: Source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, 1762. Translated by G. D. H. Cole, 1913. Book I, Chapter VI.

steps.question: Who wrote this, when, and who put it into English?
steps.line: Look closely at the source line: it has two years and two names. Which year is Rousseau's, and which is the translator's?
One long sentence. Hard words: an association is a group people join, and associate is in your KEY VOCABULARY for Day 4. Take a breath after the words each associate.

steps.question: What problem is Rousseau trying to solve, and why is it hard?
steps.line: Split the sentence after the words each associate. Find what the group must do in the first half, and what each person keeps in the second. Can both be true at once?

steps.question: Would this deal work for a person who disagrees with everyone else?
steps.line: Picture that one person. Reread the words obey himself alone, and ask what the group would do with him.

steps.question: What lasting issue does Rousseau's problem raise?
steps.line: Your clue words are the whole common force. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question fits a group holding that much force.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 5's questions in your casefile, starting on page 9. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “The problem is to find a form of association which will defend and protect with the whole common force the person and goods of each associate, and in which each, while uniting himself with all, may still obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “The problem is to find a form of association (a group that people join together). This group must defend and protect with the whole common force the person and goods of each associate. (The whole common force means the strength of everyone together. Goods means belongings. An associate is a member.) And in this group, each one joins with all the others. Each may still obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.” (To obey himself alone means to follow only his own will.)

docs.title: Rousseau distinguishes the general will from the will of all
docs.src: Source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, 1762. Translated by G. D. H. Cole, 1913. Book II, Chapter III.

steps.question: Who wrote this, and who will use his idea later?
steps.line: Same book as Document 5. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 4 says who will use this idea, and how.
One sentence, built on two terms from your KEY VOCABULARY: will of all and general will. Watch the latter and the former: the latter is the second one named, the former is the first.

steps.question: What does each kind of will care about, according to Rousseau?
steps.line: Sort his words into two columns, one for each will. What does each one take account of?

steps.question: Who gets to decide what the general will is, and what happens to people who disagree?
steps.line: Picture someone in the community who disagrees with whoever decides. Then reread what WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 4 says about 1793.

steps.question: What lasting issue could the general will raise?
steps.line: Picture a leader who claims to speak for the general will. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question fits what that leader could do.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 6's questions in your casefile, starting on page 10. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will; the latter takes account only of the common interest, while the former takes private interest into account, and is no more than a sum of particular wills.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will. The latter (the general will) takes account only of the common interest (what is good for the whole community). The former (the will of all) takes private interest (what each person wants for himself) into account. It is no more than a sum (a total, added up) of particular wills (what each single person wants).”

docs.title: Wollstonecraft on reason and the rights of women
docs.src: Source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792. Addressed to Talleyrand-Périgord, a member of the French National Assembly.

steps.question: Who is Wollstonecraft writing to, and why pick him?
steps.line: The source line's second sentence names her reader. Then find the two words she prints in capital letters, and ask what his country was writing.
Two short paragraphs, one sentence each, with pieces cut out where you see dots. In the first, she means a woman. In the second, want means lack, the way the bracket says.

steps.question: What does she demand before women can be shut out?
steps.line: Find the words prove first, and read to the end of that line. Say it in your own words.

steps.question: Whose voice is missing from the new constitution she writes about?
steps.line: Find the word excluded. Then ask who was writing the NEW CONSTITUTION, and who was left out of writing it.

steps.question: What lasting issue does she raise with the word tyrant?
steps.line: Find tyrant in her last line, and tyranny in your KEY VOCABULARY for Day 2. Then open the Six Umbrellas and see which question fits.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 7's questions in your casefile, starting on page 11. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “. . . if she be not prepared by education to become the companion of man, she will stop the progress of knowledge. . . .
“If women are to be excluded . . . prove first . . . that they want [lack] reason, else this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION will ever show that man must . . . act like a tyrant. . . .”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “. . . Suppose a woman is not prepared by education to become the companion (partner) of man. Then she will stop the progress of knowledge. . . .

“If women are to be excluded (shut out) . . . prove first . . . that they want [lack] reason (the ability to think logically). If you cannot, then this flaw (mistake) in your NEW CONSTITUTION will ever (always) show that man must . . . act like a tyrant (a ruler who uses power without limit or consent). . . .”

docs.title: Two voices from 1789: the slave trade
docs.src: Source: William Wilberforce, speech to the House of Commons, May 1789, in Cobbett, Parliamentary History of England, vol. 28 (adapted)

steps.question: Who are the two voices, and how close was each one to the slave trade?
steps.line: There are two source lines, one above each voice. For each man, ask: was he there, or was he arguing about it?

Two voices. Wilberforce speaks in two long sentences, and Equiano tells his in five shorter ones. The brackets give you the hard words, and abolition is in your KEY VOCABULARY for Day 5. Finish one voice before you start the next.

steps.question: What does each man say about the slave trade, in his own words?
steps.line: For Wilberforce, find what he says must happen and what he decided. For Equiano, follow what happened to him, sentence by sentence, to his last line.

steps.question: What can Equiano tell us that Wilberforce cannot, and who is still not heard?
steps.line: Ask what each man saw for himself. Then ask who else was there in 1789, on the ships, in the trade, or in Parliament, and is not speaking in either voice.

steps.question: What lasting issue do these two voices raise?
steps.line: Find Wilberforce's word for what the trade was founded in, and the word Equiano uses for what was done to him in his first sentence. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question those words fit.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 8's questions in your casefile, starting on page 13. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the world we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.
text: “I confess to you sir, so enormous so dreadful, so irremediable [impossible to fix] did its wickedness appear that my own mind was completely made up for the abolition. A trade founded in iniquity [wrongdoing] . . . must be abolished . . . let the consequences be what they would, I from this time determined that I would never rest till I had effected [achieved] its abolition.”
Source: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, London, 1794 edition (adapted), via OER Project

“I now saw myself deprived [robbed] of all chance of returning to my native country . . . . I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation [greeting] in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life . . . . I became so sick and low that I was not able to eat . . . . I inquired [asked] of them what was to be done with us? They gave me to understand we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “I confess to you, sir: its wickedness seemed so enormous, so dreadful, so irremediable [impossible to fix]. So my own mind was completely made up for the abolition (ending it). A trade founded in iniquity [wrongdoing] . . . must be abolished (ended) . . . . Let the consequences be what they would (no matter what happens). From this time I determined (decided) that I would never rest till I had effected [achieved] its abolition.”
Source: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, London, 1794 edition (adapted), via OER Project

“I now saw myself deprived [robbed] of all chance of returning to my native country (the land where I was born) . . . . I was soon put down under the decks. There I received such a salutation [greeting] in my nostrils (such a smell) as I had never experienced in my life . . . . I became so sick and low (weak in body and spirit) that I was not able to eat . . . . I inquired [asked] of them what was to be done with us? They gave me to understand we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”

docs.title: Catherine the Great on law and equality
docs.src: Source: Documents of Catherine the Great, W. F. Reddaway, ed., Cambridge University Press (adapted)

steps.question: Who wrote this, and what was it written for?
steps.line: The source line has no date and no name for the document. WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 6 tells you what she issued, in what year, and who it was meant to instruct.
Two sentences, each starting with dots because pieces were cut. Both are about the Laws. Hard word: framed means written.

steps.question: What does Catherine say the laws should do, and what makes citizens equal?
steps.line: Each of her two sentences answers one half. Find the word secure in the first and the word consists in the second.

steps.question: How would a serf in Catherine's Russia hear these words?
steps.line: Picture a serf hearing the words every Citizen and the same Laws read aloud. Then reread WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 6 for what happened to serfs under her rule.

steps.question: What lasting issue does a ruler writing about equality raise?
steps.line: Your clue words are Equality and the same Laws. Hold them up against WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on Day 6, then open the Six Umbrellas and see which question fits.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 9's questions in your casefile, starting on page 15. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the world we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.
text: “. . . The Laws ought to be so framed, as to secure the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible.
“. . . The Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws. . . .”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “. . . The Laws ought to be written to secure (protect) the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible.
“. . . The Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws. . . .” (Consists in this means is made of this. Subject to means ruled by.)

docs.title: Catherine's government on serfs
docs.src: Source: A Source Book for Russian History, G. Vernadsky, trans., Yale University Press, 1972 (adapted)

steps.question: Who issued this order, when, and who had to hear it?
steps.line: Read the document's first three words to find who issued it. The PARTNER TALK box under it tells you when, and the last line says where it was read.

tip.title: NO NAME ON IT?
text: Not every source tells you who made it. When it doesn't, ask three things: When was it made? Who published it, and where did it first appear? Who was it made for? Then say what the source line tells you, and what it can't.

steps.line: Three sentences, and the brackets give you the hard words. The second sentence is long: read it twice, and find who it punishes and how. Nerchinsk is a place in Siberia.

steps.question: What does the order demand of serfs, and what happens to those who complain?
steps.line: Find the words owe their landlords for the first part. For the second, read the long middle sentence twice and find who is punished and how.

steps.question: How would a serf hear this read aloud in church, and how is it different from Document 9?
steps.line: Picture a serf in church on a Sunday, hearing this. Then put it next to Catherine's words in Document 9 and say what you see.

steps.question: What lasting issue does this order raise?
steps.line: Your clue words are absolute obedience, and what happens to a serf who sends a petition. Open the Six Umbrellas and see which question those words fit.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 10's questions in your casefile, starting on page 16. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

before_we_talk.title: BEFORE WE TALK
before_we_talk.text: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the world we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.

text: “The Governing Senate . . . has deemed it necessary to make known that the landlords' serfs and peasants . . . owe their landlords proper submission and absolute obedience in all matters . . . . And should . . . any serfs and peasants . . . make bold to submit unlawful petitions [formal written complaints] complaining of their landlords, and especially to petition Her Imperial Majesty personally, then both those who make the complaints and those who write up the petitions shall be punished by the knout [a heavy whip] and forthwith deported to Nerchinsk to penal servitude [forced labor as punishment] for life . . . . it shall be read in all the churches on Sundays and holy days . . . lest anyone pretend ignorance.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “The Governing Senate (a top body of the government) . . . has decided it must make this known. The landlords' serfs and peasants . . . owe their landlords proper submission and absolute obedience in all matters . . . . (Submission means giving in. Obedience means doing what you are told.) Some serfs and peasants may . . . dare to submit unlawful petitions [formal written complaints] about their landlords. Some may even petition Her Imperial Majesty (the Empress) personally. If so, both those who make the complaints and those who write up the petitions shall be punished by the knout [a heavy whip]. And they shall be forthwith (right away) deported to Nerchinsk to penal servitude [forced labor as punishment] for life . . . . This order shall be read in all the churches on Sundays and holy days . . . lest anyone pretend ignorance (so no one can pretend they did not know).”

casefiles.title: 10.2 Casefile B · France: one revolution, in depth, 1789–1815

docs.title: Abbé Sieyès asks what the Third Estate actually is
docs.src: Source: Abbé Sieyès, 1789 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2014

steps.question: Who wrote this, and when, compared with the Estates-General meeting?
steps.line: The source line gives you the name and the year. For before or after, read the last paragraph of WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on page 3 for when the delegates met, then ask what Day 2's WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW says his pamphlet helped inspire.
Four lines: one opening sentence, then three numbered questions. Each question gets a one-word answer. The political order means the way power is shared in the government.

steps.question: What are Sieyès's three answers, and what do they say about the Third Estate?
steps.line: Each of his three words is the last word on a numbered line. Then read line 1 and line 2 side by side and ask how both can be true at once.

steps.question: How would a noble at Versailles answer Sieyès?
steps.line: Abbé is a title for a priest, so a member of the clergy is speaking up for the Third Estate. Picture a noble reading line 2. What would he say back?

text: Articles:
1. Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be founded only upon the general good.

2. The aim of all political association is the preservation of the natural and imprescriptible [inalienable] rights of man. These rights are liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression....

4. Liberty consists in the freedom to do everything which injures no one else; hence the exercise of the natural rights of each man has no limits except those which assure to the other members of the society the enjoyment of the same rights. These limits can only be determined by law....

6. Law is the expression of the general will. Every citizen has a right to participate personally, or through his representative, in its foundation. It must be the same for all, whether it protects or punishes. All citizens, being equal in the eyes of the law, are equally eligible to all dignities and to all public positions and occupations, according to their abilities, and without distinction except that of their virtues and talents....

text: Articles:
1. Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions (differences in rank) may be founded (based) only upon the general good (what is good for everyone).

2. All political association (people joining under a government) has one aim (goal). That aim is the preservation (protection) of the natural and imprescriptible [inalienable] rights of man. Inalienable means they cannot be taken away. These rights are liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression (cruel, unfair use of power)....

4. Liberty consists in the freedom to do everything which injures no one else. So the exercise (use) of the natural rights of each man has no limits, except one. The other members of society must be able to enjoy the same rights. These limits can only be determined (decided) by law....

6. Law is the expression of the general will (what is best for the whole community). Every citizen has a right to participate personally, or through his representative, in its foundation (making the law). It must be the same for all, whether it protects or punishes. All citizens are equal in the eyes of the law. So they are equally eligible (allowed) to hold all dignities (high honors), public positions and jobs. This depends on their abilities. There is no difference between them except their virtues (good qualities) and talents....

text: FIRST ARTICLE
Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights. Social distinctions can only be founded on common service.
II

The aim of all political associations is to preserve the natural and inalienable rights of Woman and Man: these are the rights to liberty, ownership, safety and, above all, resistance to oppression....
IV

Liberty and justice lie in rendering everything which belongs to others as of right. Thus the exercise of woman's natural rights has no limit other than the perpetual tyranny of man's opposing them: these limits must be reformed by the laws of natural and reason....
VI

The Law must be the expression of the general will; all citizens, female and male, should concur [agree] personally or through their representatives in its formation, and it must be the same for all. All citizens, being equal in its eyes, must be equally eligible to all honours, positions and public posts according to their abilities, and with no other distinction other than those of their virtues and talents....

text: “... Individuals are not at issue here; we are concerned with the homeland and principles. I tell you plainly: it is impossible, in this state of affairs, for the Committee to save the state; and if anyone disagrees, I will remind you just how treacherous and extensive is the scheme for bringing us down and dissolving us; how the foreigners and internal enemies have agents paid to execute it; I will remind you that faction is not dead; that it is conspiring from the depths of its dungeons; that the serpents of the Marais [a section of Paris] have not yet all been crushed....

I know we cannot flatter ourselves that we have attained perfection; but holding up a Republic surrounded by enemies, fortifying reason in favour of liberty, destroying prejudice and nullifying individual efforts against the public interest, demand moral and physical strengths that nature has perhaps denied to those who denounce us and those we are fighting....”

text: “This law, passed on 17 September 1793 [by Robespierre and the National Convention], authorized the creation of revolutionary tribunals to try those suspected of treason against the Republic and to punish those convicted with death. This legislation in effect made the penal justice system into the enforcement arm of the revolutionary government, which would now set as its primary responsibility not only the maintenance of public order but also the much more difficult and controversial task of identifying internal enemies of the Republic -- such as “profiteers” who violated the Maximum [decree to fix prices] -- and then removing them from the citizenry, where they might subvert [sabotage] the general will....”

text: “This law was passed on 17 September 1793 [by Robespierre and the National Convention]. It authorized (allowed) the creation of revolutionary tribunals (special courts). These courts would try those suspected of treason (betraying their country) against the Republic. They would punish those convicted (found guilty) with death. In effect, this legislation (law) changed the penal justice system (courts and punishment). It became the enforcement arm (the part that makes people obey) of the revolutionary government. Now the government had a primary (main) job. It was not only to keep public order. It was also the much harder and more controversial (argued-over) task of identifying internal enemies of the Republic. One example was “profiteers” who violated (broke) the Maximum [decree to fix prices]. The government would then be removing them from the citizenry (all the citizens). Among the citizens, they might subvert [sabotage] the general will....”

Unite yourselves to us, brothers, and fight with us for the same cause, etc. . . .

docs.src: Source: Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Haitian Declaration of Independence, January 1, 1804 (excerpt), from New Visions lesson G2.02.D.2

steps.question: Who is speaking now, and what changed on the island after Document 1?
steps.line: Put this date next to Document 1's date. What You Need to Know on page 3 covers the years in between. Anything there that isn't in either document can go in your OUTSIDE EVIDENCE box on page 4.
Two sentences, and the first one is long: break it at each semicolon and each set of dots. Expelled means driven out. The dots mean words were cut.

steps.question: What does Dessalines say Haiti must do now?
steps.line: Find the words that come after each we must. Then read his last sentence slowly.

steps.question: Why does Dessalines choose such strong words for the French, and why isn't freedom alone enough for him?
steps.line: Read the words around barbarians and inhuman: what does he say each one did, or still hopes to do? For the second part, read sovereignty in KEY VOCABULARY on page 3, then his last sentence.

steps.question: What lasting problem does this declaration raise? Does Document 1 raise it too?
steps.line: Pick a clue word, like re-enslaving or independent. Open the Six Umbrellas and find the question it fits. Then check Document 1 against that same umbrella.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 2's questions in your casefile, starting on page 6. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.

before_we_talk.title: BEFORE WE TALK
before_we_talk.text: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the world we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.

text: “It is not enough to have expelled the barbarians who have bloodied our land for two centuries; … We must, with one last act of national authority, forever assure the empire of liberty in the country of our birth; we must take any hope of re-enslaving us away from the inhuman government …. In the end we must live independent or die.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “It is not enough to have expelled (driven out) the barbarians (cruel, uncivilized people) who have bloodied our land for two centuries (200 years). … We must do one last act of national authority (power as a nation). With it, we must forever assure (make sure of) the empire (rule) of liberty in the country of our birth. We must take away any hope the inhuman (cruel, without pity) government has of re-enslaving us …. In the end we must live independent or die.”

docs.title: A historian on what Napoleon started in Spanish America
docs.src: Source: Robert J. Alexander, Latin America, Scholastic Book Services, from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

steps.question: Did this writer see 1808 himself, or is he writing about it later? What in the source line tells you?
steps.line: Read the source line piece by piece: a writer, a book title, a publisher. The heading above the source line has one more clue.
Two paragraphs, four sentences each. Words in [brackets] are glossed for you. A usurper is someone who grabs power that isn't rightfully theirs.

steps.question: What did Napoleon do to Spain, and how did Spanish Americans answer him?
steps.line: What Napoleon did is in the first paragraph, right where you see 1808; find every action. The second paragraph is the response: mark each thing Spanish Americans did.

steps.question: When the writer says Spanish Americans, who does he mean, and who is left out?
steps.line: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW on page 7 lists everyone in the colonies, top to bottom. Ask which of them seized control of the local governments.

steps.question: What lasting problem do the words usurper and independence point to?
steps.line: Find both words in the second paragraph. Open the Six Umbrellas and read the question under each one. Which one fits those words?

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 3's questions in your casefile, starting on page 8. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: . . . The plans and ambitions of Napoleon Bonaparte, however, did inspire the Latin Americans, although hardly in a way Napoleon expected. The French dictator invaded Spain in 1808, forced the king to abdicate [give up the throne], and presented the Spanish crown to his brother Joseph. At a stroke, Spanish America became part of the Bonaparte family empire. (A few months earlier, Napoleon had invaded Portugal, and the Portuguese royal family had fled to its colony of Brazil.)

Spanish Americans reacted sharply against this French usurper. They refused to accept Joseph Bonaparte as their king, affirmed [declared] their loyalty to the Spanish House of Bourbon, and seized control of their local governments. But almost from the beginning, the rebellion against Napoleon turned into a revolution for complete independence. There could be no turning back to the old system. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: . . . The plans and ambitions (big goals) of Napoleon Bonaparte did inspire the Latin Americans. But they did not inspire them in the way Napoleon expected. The French dictator (a ruler with total power) invaded Spain in 1808. He forced the king to abdicate [give up the throne]. Then he gave the Spanish crown to his brother Joseph. All at once, Spanish America became part of the Bonaparte family empire. (A few months earlier, Napoleon had invaded Portugal. The Portuguese royal family had fled to its colony of Brazil.)

Spanish Americans reacted sharply against this French usurper (someone who takes power that is not rightfully theirs). They refused to accept Joseph Bonaparte as their king. They affirmed [declared] their loyalty to the Spanish House of Bourbon (Spain's royal family). And they seized (took) control of their local governments. But almost from the beginning, the rebellion against Napoleon turned into a revolution for complete independence. There could be no turning back to the old system. . . .

docs.title: Simón Bolívar, the Jamaica Letter
docs.src: Source: Simón Bolívar, “Reply of a South American to a Gentleman of This Island [Jamaica],” September 6, 1815 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, August 2019

steps.question: Who is writing, to whom, and from where?
steps.line: The title in the source line says who is writing and to whom, and the bracket says where. KEY VOCABULARY on page 7 says why he was there in 1815.
Two paragraphs: five sentences, then four. Expel means drive out. The second paragraph turns toward the future at the words As soon as.

steps.question: What does Bolívar say his people need to win, and how will they get it?
steps.line: His first sentence promises to tell you, and his second sentence does. Then read on: what does he say America has, and what doesn't it have?

steps.question: Why would Bolívar tell an Englishman that America stands alone?
steps.line: Picture the reader: an Englishman on an island Britain rules. Then reread the part of the second paragraph that starts As soon as we are strong.

steps.question: What lasting problem is Bolívar trying to solve?
steps.line: Pick one clue word from Bolívar, like abandoned or attacked. Open the Six Umbrellas and find the question it fits. Then do the OUTSIDE EVIDENCE box on page 10; its hint sends you back to Day 1.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 4's questions in your casefile, starting on page 9. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: . . . I shall tell you with what we must provide ourselves in order to expel the Spaniards and to found a free government. It is union, obviously; but such union will come about through sensible planning and well-directed actions rather than by divine magic. America stands together because it is abandoned by all other nations. It is isolated in the center of the world. It has no diplomatic relations, nor does it receive any military assistance; instead, America is attacked by Spain, which has more military supplies than any we can possibly acquire through furtive [stealthy] means.

When success is not assured, when the state is weak, and when results are distantly seen, all men hesitate; opinion is divided, passions rage, and the enemy fans these passions in order to win an easy victory because of them. As soon as we are strong and under the guidance of a liberal nation which will lend us her protection, we will achieve accord [unity] in cultivating the virtues and talents that lead to glory. Then will we march majestically toward that great prosperity for which South America is destined. Then will those sciences and arts which, born in the East, have enlightened Europe, wing their way to a free Colombia, which will cordially bid them welcome. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: . . . I shall tell you what we must get for ourselves in order to expel (drive out) the Spaniards and to found (start) a free government. It is union, obviously. But such union will come from sensible planning and well-directed actions, not from divine magic (a miracle). America stands together because it is abandoned by all other nations. It is isolated (alone, cut off) in the center of the world. It has no diplomatic relations (official ties with other countries). It does not get any military help. Instead, America is attacked by Spain. Spain has more military supplies than any we can possibly get through furtive [stealthy] means.

When success is not sure, when the state is weak, and when results are far off, all men hesitate. Opinion is divided, and passions (strong feelings) rage. The enemy fans (stirs up) these passions to win an easy victory because of them. A liberal nation is one that values freedom. As soon as we are strong and under the guidance of a liberal nation that will protect us, we will achieve accord [unity]. We will build the virtues and talents that lead to glory. Then we will march majestically (grandly) toward that great prosperity (wealth and success) for which South America is destined. Then the sciences and arts, which were born in the East and have enlightened Europe, will fly to a free Colombia. Colombia will warmly welcome them. . . .

docs.title: Camillo di Cavour, 1846
docs.src: Source: Camillo di Cavour, 1846, from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2003

steps.question: Cavour wrote in 1846. Had Italy come together as one nation by then?
steps.line: Find the year What You Need to Know on page 11 gives for the Kingdom of Italy, and put it next to 1846. Then look at the word in brackets in his first line.
One long sentence, broken by two dashes. Read the part between the dashes as its own thought. Petty means small and unimportant.

steps.question: What does Cavour say Italians must set aside, and what does he hope a united Italy will become?
steps.line: Find the word silenced and read back from it to see what must go quiet. For his hope, read what comes after it, and watch for not only and above all.

steps.question: How does Cavour want Italy to come together, and how is that different from Bismarck in Document 6?
steps.line: Find the phrase here that shows how Cavour wants Italy to come together. Then open Document 6's walk and do the same for Bismarck.

steps.question: What lasting problem does the word unification point to?
steps.line: Unification is in brackets in his first line. Open the Six Umbrellas and read the question under each one. Which one fits?

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 5's questions in your casefile, starting on page 12. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: . . . Therefore, if we so ardently desire the emancipation [unification] of Italy — if we declare that in the face of this great question all the petty questions that divide us must be silenced— it is not only that we may see our country glorious and powerful but that above all we may elevate her in intelligence and moral development up to the plane of the most civilized nations. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: . . . Therefore, we so ardently (strongly) desire the emancipation [unification] of Italy. We declare that in the face of this great question, all the petty questions that divide us must be silenced. We do this not only so that we may see our country glorious and powerful. Above all, we do it so that we may elevate (raise) her in intelligence and moral development. We want to raise her up to the plane (level) of the most civilized nations. . . .

docs.title: Otto von Bismarck (adapted)
docs.src: Source: Otto von Bismarck (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam

steps.question: When did Bismarck say this, and who was he talking to?
steps.line: This source line has no date and no audience. Find Bismarck in What You Need to Know on page 11.
One sentence in two halves: what will not reach the goal, then what will. Read each half on its own. Democracy means rule by the people, through voting.

steps.question: What does Bismarck say will not reach his goal, and what will?
steps.line: Say his sentence back in your own words. Then ask what blood and iron could stand for.

steps.question: How is Bismarck's way different from what Cavour hopes for in Document 5?
steps.line: Bismarck's sentence names what he won't use and what he will. Put that next to the phrase you found in Cavour.

steps.question: What lasting problem does Bismarck's plan raise?
steps.line: Take his last three words, or a clue word from Cavour, and open the Six Umbrellas. Which question do they fit? Then do the OUTSIDE EVIDENCE box on page 13.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 6's questions in your casefile, starting on page 12. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
text: “Not by democracy or liberal standards will our goal be achieved but by blood and iron.”

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: “Our goal will not be achieved (reached) by democracy or liberal standards (the rules of a free government). It will be achieved by blood and iron.”

docs.title: Map: the peoples of Austria-Hungary, 1911
docs.src: Source: William R. Shepherd, “Distribution of Races in Austria-Hungary,” Historical Atlas, Henry Holt, 1911 (public domain)

steps.question: Who made this map, when, and what do its colors stand for?
steps.line: The title runs sideways down the right edge. The date is in the source line, and the note under it tells you what Races means here.
Start with the legend in the lower left and read every name. Then find the heavy black border and look at the colors inside it. Big capital letters are regions; small ones are cities.

steps.question: Which peoples live inside the empire's border, and what could that mean for one emperor ruling them all?
steps.line: Read every name in the legend and find each color inside the heavy border. Then reread What You Need to Know on page 14, especially the question the other peoples asked.

steps.question: How would one of these peoples see this map in 1911?
steps.line: Pick one people from the legend and look at the map as one of them would. Where does your color sit, and whose border is drawn around it?

steps.question: What lasting problem does this map raise?
steps.line: Look at how long the legend's list of names is. Open the Six Umbrellas and ask which question that list could answer. Then look at Document 8.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 7's questions in your casefile, starting on page 15. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: “Races” in 1911 meant groups of people who spoke the same language. The colors show languages.

docs.title: “The Boiling Point,” Punch, October 2, 1912
docs.src: Source: Leonard Raven-Hill, “The Boiling Point,” Punch (London), October 2, 1912 (public domain)

steps.question: Where and when was this cartoon printed, and what happened soon after?
steps.line: The source line says where Punch was printed and when. Then read the note under it. Did the cartoonist know what was coming when he drew this?
Read the words first: the caption at the bottom and the two words on the pot. Then the men, one at a time, left to right: look at each hat. Then the edges of the picture.

steps.question: What does the cartoonist think is about to happen, and which two details show it?
steps.line: Put the caption and the words on the pot together. Then look at the steam and at what the men are doing with their hands. How long can that last?

steps.question: Who does the cartoonist put on top of the pot, and who isn't shown at all?
steps.line: The note under the source line names who is on the lid. Then check Balkans in Day 4's KEY VOCABULARY on page 14: are any of those peoples drawn here?

steps.question: What lasting problem is boiling in this pot?
steps.line: Start with the two words on the pot. Open the Six Umbrellas and find the question they fit. Then do the OUTSIDE EVIDENCE box on page 17.
